lead: This unit takes a transistor from a safe DC operating point to a working amplifier. After it you can set and stabilise the bias of a BJT or a MOSFET, replace the device with a small-signal model, and compute gain, input resistance and output resistance for CE, CB, CC, CS, CG and CD stages. You can also couple stages into a multistage amplifier and read the cascode and the Darlington pair as two-transistor building blocks.
about: This unit moves from holding a transistor at the right DC point to making it amplify. Chapter 2.1 fixes that point with the DC load line and asks why it drifts with temperature and β. Chapters 2.2 and 2.3 build the standard bias networks, first for BJTs and then for JFETs and MOSFETs. Chapter 2.4 replaces the transistor by a small-signal model: h-parameter, hybrid-π or T. Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 use those models to get gain, input resistance and output resistance for the CE, CB, CC and CS, CG, CD stages. Chapter 2.7 couples stages together, and Chapter 2.8 stacks two transistors into the cascode and the Darlington pair.

chapters.idea: Every amplifier needs a fixed DC current and voltage chosen on the DC load line, and that choice must not wander when temperature or β changes.
chapters.depth: Draw the DC load line on the output characteristics: it runs from I_C(sat) = V_CC/R_C on the current axis to V_CE(cutoff) = V_CC on the voltage axis. The crossing with the base-current curve is the operating point; some syllabi call it the quiescent point or Q-point. Cover cutoff, active and saturation regions, how R_C and V_CC move the line, bias stabilization and the three stability factors S = ∂I_C/∂I_CO, S' = ∂I_C/∂V_BE and S'' = ∂I_C/∂β, thermal runaway, and the Early effect as base-width modulation that tilts the output curves and produces r_o. Stop before the AC load line.

figure.title: DC load line and Q-point
figure.caption: The straight load line drops from 6 mA to 12 V; the operating point sits where the 47 microampere curve cuts it, near 2.6 V and 4.7 mA.
figure.aria: A load line falling from 6 milliamperes at zero volts to zero current at 12 volts, crossed by two flat output curves at 4.71 and 2.36 milliamperes.

chapters.example: A silicon npn transistor has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 2 kΩ, R_B = 240 kΩ and β = 100. Take V_BE = 0.7 V. (a) Find I_B, I_C and V_CE. (b) Draw the DC load line and mark the Q-point. (c) Say whether the transistor is in the active region. Answer: I_B = (12 − 0.7)/240 kΩ = 47.1 µA; I_C = 100 × 47.1 µA = 4.71 mA; V_CE = 12 − 4.71 mA × 2 kΩ = 12 − 9.42 = 2.58 V. The line ends at I_C(sat) = 6 mA and V_CE(cutoff) = 12 V, so Q = (2.58 V, 4.71 mA). V_CE = 2.58 V > 0.3 V, so the device is in the active region, but the margin above saturation is small.
chapters.trap: Assuming a Q-point is in the active region without checking V_CE against V_CE(sat). Another common slip is drawing the DC load line using the collector resistor in parallel with the load, which is the AC load line and belongs to a later unit.
chapters.prereq: BJT structure, regions of operation and output characteristics from the devices course; Unit 1 for the DC supply that sets V_CC.
chapters.leave: AC load line, swing and bandwidth to Unit 3; the small-signal model to Chapter 2.4.

chapters.idea: Three resistor networks hold the BJT operating point, and the voltage divider wins because its Q-point barely moves when β changes.
chapters.depth: Fixed bias (base resistor, also called base bias) with S = 1 + β; collector-to-base feedback bias, also called collector feedback bias, where R_B returns to the collector; voltage divider bias, also called self-bias or emitter bias, with R_E bypassed by a capacitor; and emitter-stabilized bias, which keeps R_E unbypassed. For each: draw the circuit, write the DC loop equations, find I_C and V_CE, and quote the stability factor. Teach the 10× rule for the divider current and a five-step design sequence. Compare the three in one table of S and of I_C change when β doubles. State V_BE ≈ 0.7 V for silicon and name the alternatives.

figure.title: Designing voltage divider bias
figure.caption: The divider fixes the base voltage, the emitter resistor turns it into a current, and the last step is always a check that the transistor stays in the active region.
figure.aria: A top-down flow of five steps: supply, base voltage from the divider, emitter current set by the emitter resistor, collector current, and a final check of collector-emitter voltage.

chapters.example: A voltage divider bias circuit has V_CC = 12 V, R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, β = 100 and V_BE = 0.7 V. (a) Find the Q-point. (b) Check the 10× rule. (c) Find I_C if β rises to 200. Answer: V_B = 12 × 10/(47 + 10) = 2.105 V; V_E = 2.105 − 0.7 = 1.405 V; I_E = 1.405 V/1 kΩ = 1.405 mA; I_C ≈ 1.4 mA; V_C = 12 − 1.4 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 8.92 V; V_CE = 8.92 − 1.405 = 7.52 V. Divider current = 2.105 V/10 kΩ = 210 µA, about 15 times I_B = 14 µA, so the rule holds. With β = 200 the base current halves, V_B moves by a few tens of millivolts and I_C stays close to 1.4 mA. Fixed bias with the same transistor would double I_C.
chapters.trap: Applying the divider formula V_B = V_CC R2/(R1 + R2) when the base current is not small compared with the divider current, and forgetting that V_E, not V_B, is what sets the current.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the load line and the stability factors.
chapters.leave: Current mirrors and active loads to Unit 5; how the bias current sets gain to Chapters 2.4 and 2.5.

chapters.idea: A FET needs a gate-source voltage, not a base current, so its bias circuits work from the transfer characteristic and a bias line drawn on it.
chapters.depth: JFET self-bias with R_S and V_G = 0; fixed bias with a separate gate battery; voltage divider bias at the gate; the same three ideas for the depletion MOSFET, whose V_GS may be positive or negative. For the enhancement MOSFET teach gate divider plus source resistor, and drain-to-gate feedback bias. For all of them, solve the quadratic from Shockley's equation I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² or the square law I_D = K_n(V_GS − V_TN)², then draw the bias line I_D = (V_G − V_GS)/R_S and mark the intersection. Finish with the saturation check V_DS > V_GS − V_TN.

figure.title: Self-bias point of a JFET
figure.caption: The parabola is the device and the straight line is the 1 kilohm source resistor; they meet at V_GS = −3 V and I_D = 3 mA.
figure.aria: A downward parabola for drain current against gate-source voltage from 12 milliamperes at zero volts to zero at minus 6 volts, crossing a straight rising bias line at minus 3 volts and 3 milliamperes.

chapters.example: A JFET has I_DSS = 12 mA and V_P = −6 V. It is self-biased with R_S = 1 kΩ and R_D = 2 kΩ from V_DD = 20 V. Find V_GS, I_D, V_D, V_S and V_DS, and check the region. Answer: I_D = −V_GS/R_S = −V_GS/1 kΩ, and I_D = 12 mA (1 − V_GS/(−6 V))². Substituting gives 12(1 + V_GS/6)² = −V_GS with V_GS in volts and I_D in milliamperes. Solving, V_GS = −3 V or V_GS = −12 V; the second lies beyond pinch-off, so reject it. Then I_D = 3 mA. V_S = 3 mA × 1 kΩ = 3 V, V_D = 20 − 3 mA × 2 kΩ = 14 V, V_DS = 11 V. Here V_GS − V_P = 3 V and V_DS = 11 V, so the JFET is in saturation.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign of V_GS = −I_D R_S wrong, and keeping both roots of the quadratic when one of them lies outside the valid region. For an enhancement NMOS, forgetting that V_GS and V_TN are both positive.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for load-line thinking; FET construction, the transfer characteristic and the square law from the devices course.
chapters.leave: MOSFET current sources and active loads to Unit 5; small-signal MOSFET parameters and stage gains to Chapter 2.6.

chapters.idea: For small signals the transistor becomes a linear two-port, and the h-parameter, hybrid-π and T forms are the same device written three ways.
chapters.depth: Define the four h-parameters from the two-port equations: h_ie = input resistance with output shorted, h_fe = forward current gain with output shorted, h_re = reverse voltage feedback with input open, h_oe = output admittance with input open. Build the h-parameter equivalent circuit and the CE approximate model that drops h_re and h_oe. Then the hybrid-π (some syllabi call it the Giacoletto model): r_π, g_m, r_o, C_π, C_µ and the base spreading resistance r_x, with g_m = I_C/V_T, r_π = β/g_m, r_o = V_A/I_C, V_T ≈ 26 mV at room temperature. Then the T-model with r_e = α/g_m ≈ 26 mV/I_E. Show the conversions numerically. Only a few universities teach the full T-model with r_x; keep that part short.

figure.title: One device, three models
figure.caption: All three boxes describe the same transistor at the same operating point; only the numbers you are given change.
figure.aria: Four boxes left to right: the biased transistor, its h-parameter two-port, the hybrid-pi model and the T-model, joined by conversion arrows.

chapters.example: An npn transistor is biased at I_C = 1 mA with β = 100 and Early voltage V_A = 100 V. Take V_T = 26 mV. (a) Find g_m, r_π and r_o. (b) With R_L = 5 kΩ and r_o included, find the intrinsic voltage gain. (c) Write the h-parameters of the same device. Answer: g_m = I_C/V_T = 1 mA/26 mV = 38.5 mS; r_π = β/g_m = 100/38.5 mS = 2.6 kΩ; r_o = V_A/I_C = 100 V/1 mA = 100 kΩ. R_L ∥ r_o = 5 kΩ ∥ 100 kΩ = 4.76 kΩ, so A_v = −g_m(R_L ∥ r_o) = −38.5 mS × 4.76 kΩ = −183. In h-parameter terms h_fe = β = 100, h_ie = r_π = 2.6 kΩ, h_oe = 1/r_o = 10 µS and h_re is small enough to neglect.
chapters.trap: Mixing values from two models, for example putting h_ie where the hybrid-π needs r_π while using a different bias current, and dropping the minus sign on the CE gain.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2 for the DC current that fixes g_m, r_π and r_e.
chapters.leave: Miller effect, C_π and C_µ at high frequency, and cut-off frequencies to Unit 3; small-signal models of the differential pair to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The same transistor gives three different amplifiers depending on which terminal is grounded for the signal.
chapters.depth: For CE, CB and CC: draw the circuit, replace the device by its model, and derive A_v, A_i, R_in and R_out, with and without a bypassed emitter resistor. For CE use A_v = −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e and R_in = R1 ∥ R2 ∥ β r_e; for CB give the low input resistance, unity current gain and no phase inversion; for CC, the emitter follower, derive A_v = (R_E ∥ R_L)/(r_e + R_E ∥ R_L) close to 1 and the very low output resistance. Cover phase, typical use of each stage (the emitter follower as a buffer driving a cable or a small speaker), and a short table of gain and resistance. Keep the cut-off frequencies for later.

figure.title: One transistor, three connections
figure.caption: The common-emitter stage inverts and gives voltage gain; the emitter follower gives no voltage gain but the lowest output resistance of the three.
figure.aria: A four-row table of voltage gain, current gain, input resistance, output resistance and phase for the common-emitter, common-base and common-collector connections.

chapters.example: A CE amplifier has I_C = 1 mA, β = 100, R_C = 3 kΩ, R_L = 6 kΩ and bias resistors R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ. Take V_T = 26 mV and ignore r_o. Find r_e, A_v, R_in and R_out. Answer: r_e = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω. R_C ∥ R_L = 3 kΩ ∥ 6 kΩ = 2 kΩ, so A_v = −2000/26 = −76.9, a phase shift of 180°. The base input resistance is β r_e = 2.6 kΩ; R1 ∥ R2 = 8.25 kΩ; so R_in = 8.25 kΩ ∥ 2.6 kΩ = 1.98 kΩ. R_out ≈ R_C = 3 kΩ. The same transistor as a CC stage with R_E = 2 kΩ gives A_v = 2000/(26 + 2000) = 0.987 and R_out ≈ r_e + (R1 ∥ R2 ∥ R_S)/β, a few tens of ohms.
chapters.trap: Writing R_out of the emitter follower as high because it looks like a collector resistor, and forgetting the 180° inversion of CE when adding stage gains in cascade.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for the hybrid-π and T-models.
chapters.leave: Lower and upper cut-off frequencies and gain-bandwidth product to Unit 3; feedback around these stages to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Replace the base with a gate and the same three connections give CS, CG and CD, but the gate current is zero, so input resistance stops being a design problem.
chapters.depth: Small-signal MOSFET model with g_m = 2√(K_n I_D) for the square law, g_m = 2 I_D/(V_GS − V_TN), and r_o = 1/(λ I_D). Then CS: A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ R_L ∥ r_o), very high input resistance; CG: low input resistance, current gain near 1, no inversion; CD, the source follower: A_v = g_m R_s/(1 + g_m R_s) below 1, low output resistance. Show a sample gain and frequency-response sketch comparing CS and CD. Mention the body effect and that only a few universities teach it in depth.

figure.title: Gain against frequency
figure.caption: Both stages are flat at 40 dB in the middle band; the source follower keeps its gain two decades further before rolling off.
figure.aria: Two gain curves that are flat at 40 decibels and then fall; the common-source curve starts falling near 100 kilohertz, the source-follower curve near 10 megahertz.

chapters.example: An NMOS CS amplifier has K_n = 1 mA/V², V_TN = 1 V, λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, I_D = 1 mA, R_D = 10 kΩ and R_L = 10 kΩ. (a) Find g_m and r_o. (b) Find A_v. (c) Find A_v for the same device as a source follower with R_s = 1 kΩ. Answer: V_GS − V_TN = √(I_D/K_n) = √(1 mA/1 mA/V²) = 1 V; g_m = 2√(K_n I_D) = 2√(1 × 1) mS = 2 mS; r_o = 1/(λ I_D) = 1/(0.02 × 1 mA) = 50 kΩ. R_D ∥ R_L = 5 kΩ; 5 kΩ ∥ 50 kΩ = 4.55 kΩ; A_v = −2 mS × 4.55 kΩ = −9.1. For the source follower A_v = g_m R_s/(1 + g_m R_s) = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.667.
chapters.trap: Using the BJT formula r_e = 26 mV/I_E for a FET, and forgetting λ so that r_o is left out when it is comparable to R_D. For an enhancement device, also forgetting that V_GS must be larger than V_TN.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for the bias point and the square law; Chapter 2.4 for the idea of a small-signal model.
chapters.leave: Body effect, high-frequency MOSFET capacitance and cut-off frequencies to Unit 3; CMOS stages and active loads to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Single stages are too weak, so they are chained, and the way you join them decides gain, bandwidth and whether DC gets through.
chapters.depth: RC coupling: coupling capacitor blocks DC, gain per stage multiplies, bandwidth shrinks; direct coupling: no capacitor, DC levels shift and drift, used inside op-amps; transformer coupling: impedance matching and DC isolation, but bulky and narrow band. Give total gain in dB, A_total = A1 × A2 × ... and A(dB) = 20 log₁₀|A|. For n identical stages give the bandwidth shrinkage f_L' = f_L/√(2^(1/n) − 1) and f_H' = f_H × √(2^(1/n) − 1). Compare the three types in a table.

figure.caption: Each branch is a coupling method and each child is the property that decides where the method is used.
figure.aria: A tree with multistage coupling at the root and three children, RC coupled, transformer and direct, each with a short note on its trade-off.

chapters.example: Two identical RC-coupled stages each have midband gain 50 and cut-off frequencies f_L = 50 Hz and f_H = 200 kHz. (a) Find the overall gain in dB. (b) Find the overall lower and upper cut-off frequencies. Answer: A_total = 50 × 50 = 2500, so A(dB) = 20 log₁₀ 2500 = 68 dB. For n = 2, √(2^(1/2) − 1) = √0.4142 = 0.6436. Then f_L' = 50/0.6436 = 77.7 Hz and f_H' = 200 × 0.6436 = 128.7 kHz. The bandwidth falls from 199.95 kHz to 128.6 kHz, so cascading raised the gain but narrowed the band.
chapters.trap: Adding gains in dB but multiplying them as plain numbers in the same line, and thinking that cascading identical stages leaves the cut-off frequencies unchanged.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 for single-stage gain, input and output resistance.
chapters.leave: The full Bode treatment of cascaded stages and the Miller effect to Unit 3; the direct-coupled cascade inside an op-amp to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two transistors can be joined so that one cancels the other's weakness: the cascode buys bandwidth, the Darlington buys current gain.
chapters.depth: Cascode: a CE stage feeding a CB stage, also called a common-emitter common-base pair. Derive A_v ≈ −g_m1 R_L, the very high output resistance, and the small Miller capacitance that keeps the input pole far out. Darlington: two CC stages, also called a Darlington pair, with β_D = β1 β2, V_BE(total) ≈ 1.4 V, R_in ≈ β_D R_E and the first transistor never reaching saturation. Give the emitter-follower use as a buffer and the cascode use as a wideband stage. Mention the complementary Darlington, some syllabi call it the Sziklai pair, in one line. Only a few universities teach the cascode's frequency analysis here.

figure.title: Two compound pairs
figure.caption: The upper chain stacks a common-emitter on a common-base stage; the lower chain stacks two emitter followers and multiplies their current gains.
figure.aria: Two signal chains from a common input: one through a common-emitter then common-base stage to a high-gain output, the other through two emitter followers to a high input-resistance output.

chapters.example: A Darlington pair has β1 = β2 = 100, R_E = 100 Ω and an emitter current of 100 mA. (a) Find β_D and the base current. (b) Find the input resistance at the base. (c) Find the base voltage needed. Answer: β_D = 100 × 100 = 10,000; I_B = 100 mA/10,000 = 10 µA. R_in ≈ β_D R_E = 10,000 × 100 Ω = 1 MΩ. V_B = 2 V_BE + I_E R_E = 1.4 V + 100 mA × 100 Ω = 1.4 + 10 = 11.4 V, so the supply must be comfortably above 11.4 V. For comparison, a single transistor with β = 100 would need I_B = 1 mA and R_in ≈ 10 kΩ.
chapters.trap: Writing β_D = β1 + β2 instead of β1β2, and forgetting that the Darlington needs about 1.4 V between base and emitter, which eats headroom in a low-voltage supply.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.5 and 2.7 for stage gains and for what cascading does to bandwidth.
chapters.leave: The cascode and folded-cascode current sources and op-amp input stages to Unit 5; the full high-frequency treatment to Unit 3.
